questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Three tissue systems in a vascular plant
questions.learningObjective: name the three tissue systems of a vascular plant and the job of each
questions.stem: A transverse section of a young dicot stem shows three tissue systems arranged as layers. Which pairing gives each system its role?

options.text: Dermal tissue covers the surface, vascular tissue transports, and ground tissue fills and supports
Dermal tissue transports, vascular tissue fills and supports, and ground tissue covers the surface
options.misconception: swaps the dermal and ground roles and puts transport on the outer layer

options.text: Dermal tissue stores starch, vascular tissue makes sugars, and ground tissue defends against insects
options.misconception: assigns storage, photosynthesis and defence, which none of the three systems does as its main job

options.text: Dermal tissue moves water up, vascular tissue moves sugar up, and ground tissue anchors the plant in soil
options.misconception: treats the three systems as three transport routes and forgets the covering function

questions.explanation: The dermal system is the outer covering, one cell layer or a cuticle and epidermis over the whole plant, and its job is to control exchange and loss. The vascular system is the transport tissue: xylem carries water and minerals, phloem carries sugars. The ground system fills the space between, storing starch, supporting mechanically and providing the medium in which vascular tissue sits. The belief that all three are transport routes fails because only one of them, the vascular system, carries anything over long distances, and the belief that ground tissue defends the plant fails because chemical defence is a property of individual cells rather than a tissue layer.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three is even a continuous sheath over the whole plant.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Xylem and phloem as separate conduits
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the direction and the cargo of the two vascular conduits
questions.stem: A cut stem stands in coloured water and the colour appears in the leaves. A second identical stem is fed sugar labelled with a marker. What do the two results show?

options.text: Both conduits carried both substances at once, in opposite directions along the same tubes
options.misconception: believes one tube network transports water and sugar together in opposite directions

options.text: Xylem carried the coloured water upward and phloem carried the labelled sugar between sources and sinks
Xylem carried the sugar and phloem carried the water, so the two results test opposite routes
options.misconception: reverses the cargo of the two conduits, which is the classic first-year reversal

options.text: Neither conduit transported anything, and both results came from diffusion through dead wall material
options.misconception: rules out transport because the mature xylem cells are dead, forgetting that flow still occurs

questions.explanation: The two conduits are separate systems with different cargoes and different mechanisms. Xylem is a set of dead-ended tubes that move water and dissolved minerals from the root to the shoot, driven by a tension the leaf creates. Phloem is living sieve tissue, with companion cells and loading proteins, that moves sugars from where they are made or stored to where they are used or stored. The belief that the two share tubes fails because a vessel and a sieve tube have different wall structure and different contents, and the belief that the deadness of xylem prevents transport fails because dead conduits can still conduct a pressure-driven flow perfectly well.
questions.hint: Ask which system has living contents with nuclei-free sieve plates.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Vascular bundles: ring versus scattered arrangement
questions.learningObjective: connect bundle arrangement to the capacity for secondary growth
questions.stem: A dicot stem section shows vascular bundles in a ring near the outside. A maize stem section shows them scattered through the ground tissue. What follows from that?

options.text: Both thicken equally, because bundle position in the section makes no difference to growth
options.misconception: ignores the cambium and assumes arrangement alone cannot limit thickening

options.text: Only the scattered stem normally thickens, because scattered bundles are fed by more phloem
options.misconception: believes the number of bundles controls the thickening rather than the presence of a cambium

options.text: Only the ringed stem normally thickens, because a continuous cambium layer can link the bundles
Neither thickens, because a ring of bundles is too rigid and a scattering is too loose
options.misconception: reads mechanical stiffness rather than the presence or absence of a lateral meristem

questions.explanation: A ring of bundles places the xylem of each bundle on the inside and the phloem on the outside, so a layer of dividing cells, the vascular cambium, can form in the continuous plane between them and add secondary xylem inwards. Scattered bundles have no such shared plane, so there is usually no vascular cambium and no ordinary thickening. The claim that arrangement is irrelevant fails because the cambium needs a continuous ring to work as one sheet, and the belief that a ring is too rigid fails because a young ring of separate bundles is not a closed circle of wood.
questions.hint: Ask what a lateral meristem needs in order to form one continuous sheet.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: classify a plant from a set of linked features
questions.stem: A plant has one cotyledon, parallel leaf venation, scattered stem bundles, and a flower whose parts number three. What does that combination identify?

options.text: A dicot, because scattered bundles are common and the part count of three proves nothing
options.misconception: thinks a single numeric feature can never be diagnostic in a classification key

options.text: A dicot, because one seed leaf and parallel venation are the two most useful features
options.misconception: knows one of the four features but assigns it to the wrong group

options.text: A monocot, because scattered bundles and a part count of three override the other two features
options.misconception: treats the four features as independent instead of mutually supporting

options.text: A monocot, because one seed leaf and parallel venation go with scattered bundles and threes

questions.explanation: The four features move together, which is what makes them useful. Monocots have a single cotyledon, parallel venation, scattered bundles, and flower parts in threes; the dicot group has two cotyledons, netted venation, bundles in a ring, and parts in fours or fives. Because the features covary, one feature that is hard to observe can be checked against another. The claim that one seed leaf identifies a dicot fails because the number of cotyledons is exactly the feature that separates the groups, and the claim that a part count of three proves nothing fails because a count of three rather than four or five is one of the most reliable single characters in the key.
questions.hint: Ask whether the four observations could belong to two different plants.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Root cap protection at the tip
questions.learningObjective: state what the root cap protects the growing tip from
questions.stem: The tip of a root is covered by a thimble of tissue whose outer cells are continually sloughed away as the root pushes down. What is that cap for?

options.text: Desiccation, by secreting a waterproofing layer onto the root surface
options.misconception: confuses the root cap's mucous layer with the cuticle that limits water loss

options.text: Abrasion, by shedding cells that are worn away against soil particles
Nitrate uptake, by converting soil nitrate into ammonium for the root
options.misconception: moves nitrogen assimilation, a leaf function, into the root cap

options.text: Root-hair growth, by holding back the hairs so they stay short and firm
options.misconception: treats the cap as a brake on absorptive hairs rather than a wear shield

questions.explanation: A root tip pushing between soil grains is abraded continuously, so the cap is built from cells that are cheap to replace and are discarded as they wear. The cap also senses gravity: dense plastids, amyloplasts, settle in the central cells and the tissue reports which way is down, which is how the root curves after it is turned sideways. The belief that the cap prevents drying fails because the cuticle and the epidermis do that work and the cap has no waterproofing role, and the belief that it restrains root hairs fails because hairs arise further up the root, behind the zone of elongation.
questions.hint: Ask what a tissue that is deliberately discarded has in common with a worn tyre tread.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Root hairs and absorption surface area
questions.learningObjective: compute how much extra absorbing area root hairs add
questions.stem: A 10 cm length of root of radius 0.3 mm carries hairs 1.5 mm long and 0.06 mm across at 40 hairs per square centimetre of root. By what factor do the hairs increase the surface available to absorb water and minerals?

options.text: About 4.3 times, because the count of hairs is added directly to the root's area
options.misconception: adds a dimensionless count to an area and doubles the result a second time

options.text: About 1.1 times, because the hairs spread over the same 1.88 square centimetres
options.misconception: assumes the hairs reuse the root's own surface instead of adding a new one

options.text: About 2.1 times, because the hairs add 2.13 square centimetres to 1.88 square centimetres
About 1.0 times, because a cylinder has the same surface as the root beneath it
options.misconception: believes the two surfaces coincide, forgetting that a hair sticks out from the root

questions.explanation: The root itself presents 2 times pi times 0.03 cm times 10 cm, which is 1.885 square centimetres. At 40 hairs per square centimetre that root carries 75.4 hairs, and each hair has a lateral area of pi times 0.006 cm times 1.5 cm, which is 0.0283 square centimetres, so the hairs contribute 2.13 square centimetres. Adding gives 4.02 square centimetres, which is 2.13 times the original, and the ratio route gives the same figure directly as 1 plus 40 times 0.0283, which is 2.13. The belief that the increase is only a tenth fails because it treats the hairs as a coat on the same surface rather than tubes projecting away from it.
questions.hint: Convert the radius to centimetres before using the cylinder formula, then add the two areas.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Water potential and its two components
questions.learningObjective: combine solute and pressure potentials into a water potential
questions.stem: Water potential has a pressure term and a solute term, and the two sum to give the drive for water movement. What signs do they carry in a turgid plant cell?

options.text: Pressure is positive and solute potential is negative, so a cell can hold both at once
Both are positive, because dissolved particles increase the drive for water to move
options.misconception: believes solute raises water potential instead of lowering it

options.text: Pressure is negative and solute potential is positive, so the two signs are swapped
options.misconception: swaps the two signs, which is the most common single-term error

options.text: Both are negative, because the cell wall resists any water held inside the cell
options.misconception: confuses the wall's restraining force with the sign of the internal pressure

questions.explanation: A cell that has taken up water presses outward on its wall, and that outward pressure is positive, so pressure potential is positive. Dissolved solutes lower the chemical potential of the water, so the solute term is negative. The two normally partly cancel: a cell with a solute potential of -0.50 megapascals and a pressure potential of +0.40 megapascals has a water potential of -0.10 megapascals, and water will still enter it from a solution at -0.30 megapascals. The belief that solutes raise water potential fails because adding solute makes water less free to move out, and the belief that both terms are negative fails because a turgid cell is under genuine internal pressure.
questions.hint: Ask which direction each term pushes, and in which direction solutes push it.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: compute a solute potential from a molarity and a temperature
questions.stem: The sap of a plant cell has a total solute concentration of 0.20 moles per litre, counted as separate particles, at 25 degrees Celsius. Using the gas constant in litre atmospheres per mole per kelvin, what is the solute potential?

options.text: About -4.9 atmospheres, which is the same product left in atmosphere units
options.misconception: computes the right product in the wrong pressure unit and never converts it

options.text: About -0.0050 megapascals, from the same product divided by one thousand twice over
options.misconception: converts litres to cubic metres and then to pascals, so the unit is wrong twice

options.text: About +0.50 megapascals, because dissolved particles raise the water potential
options.misconception: gets the magnitude right and the sign wrong, a sign convention slip

options.text: About -0.50 megapascals, from 0.20 times 0.0821 times 298 converted to pascals

questions.explanation: The solute potential is minus the van 't Hoff term: minus the concentration in moles per cubic metre times the gas constant 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin times 298 kelvin. A concentration of 0.20 moles per litre is 200 moles per cubic metre, so the result is minus 200 times 8.314 times 298 pascals, which is minus 495,500 pascals, or minus 0.496 megapascals. Repeating the same product with the constant written as 0.0821 litre atmospheres per mole per kelvin and one atmosphere taken as 0.101325 megapascals gives 0.20 times 0.0821 times 298 times 0.101325, again minus 0.496 megapascals. The figure of 4.89 is the same arithmetic before the unit conversion, and the double-thousand error shows up as minus 0.0050.
questions.hint: Work in joules and pascals: convert 0.20 moles per litre to 200 moles per cubic metre first.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Sap concentration as water leaves a cell
questions.learningObjective: predict how a solute potential changes as a cell loses water
questions.stem: A flaccid plant cell has a solute potential of -0.90 megapascals. It is put in a hypertonic solution and loses water until its volume is half what it was, with all the solute still inside. What is its solute potential then?

options.text: -0.90 megapascals, because the potential depends only on which solute is dissolved
options.misconception: believes solute potential ignores concentration entirely and depends on identity alone

options.text: -0.45 megapascals, because halving the volume halves the concentration of a fixed solute
options.misconception: inverts the concentration change, treating a smaller volume as a weaker solution

options.text: -1.80 megapascals, because halving the volume doubles the concentration of a fixed amount of solute
-3.60 megapascals, because halving the volume quadruples the concentration of the solute
options.misconception: applies the square of the volume ratio to a linear concentration relationship

questions.explanation: The amount of solute is fixed, so concentration rises as the inverse of volume: halving the volume doubles the concentration, and the solute potential is directly proportional to concentration, so it doubles as well, from -0.90 to -1.80 megapascals. Recovering the molarity independently gives 0.363 moles per litre from the 0.90 megapascals, and 0.727 moles per litre at half the volume, which multiplied by the same constant returns -1.80. A cell with that value and a pressure potential of +0.30 would need a water potential of -1.50 megapascals, which a living cell cannot sustain, so the membrane pulls away from the wall and the cell becomes plasmolysed instead of pressing harder.
questions.hint: Amount of solute divided by volume is concentration, and the potential scales with concentration.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain what pulls a water column up a tall conduit
questions.stem: Water reaches the top of a tall tree, far higher than capillarity in a narrow glass tube of the same bore would lift it. Which property of water and of the conduit accounts for that?

options.text: The width of the conduits, since a wide tube always carries water higher than a narrow one
options.misconception: believes lumen diameter sets the maximum height instead of the tension available

options.text: Active pumping by living cells in the xylem, powered by sugars made in the crown
options.misconception: assumes water is actively pumped up the trunk, ignoring that mature conduits are dead

options.text: The absence of any resistance inside a tube whose walls are already dead at maturity
options.misconception: treats the deadness of the conduit as the driving force rather than a neutral fact

options.text: Cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to the wall, pulled upward by a tension set at the leaf

questions.explanation: Evaporation from the wet walls of a leaf lowers the pressure in the finest xylem conduits, and that negative pressure is transmitted down the column as a tension. Water molecules cohere to one another and adhere to the conduit wall, so the whole column is pulled up rather than each molecule climbing alone, and the column stands at whatever height the tension balances. Because the tension is transmitted through the water itself, the height limit has nothing to do with bore diameter. The belief that living cells pump water fails because mature xylem vessels and tracheids have no protoplast, and the belief that deadness is the driving force fails because deadness only removes living resistance, it supplies no energy.
questions.hint: Ask where the energy for lifting comes from, and follow the pressure change upward.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: account for the fall in water potential along the soil-root-leaf pathway
questions.stem: Water moves in one direction through soil, root, stem, leaf and finally air. What makes the water potential fall at each step of that route?

options.text: Gravity alone, because the solute term is the same in every tissue along the route
options.misconception: assumes a single mechanism accounts for the whole gradient and misses the osmotic term

options.text: Solute and gravity in the soil, the cost of lifting in the xylem, then evaporation into drier air
Evaporation in the leaf alone, because every step below the leaf is already at one potential
options.misconception: believes the whole gradient is created at the end of the pathway

options.text: The solute term alone, because air holds water so tightly that it pulls hardest of all
options.misconception: reverses the sizes, treating dry air as the weakest step in the chain

questions.explanation: The gradient is built up in stages. Soil water has a solute potential set by dissolved salts, and moving up the xylem adds a gravitational cost that is small per metre but accumulates over the height of the plant. At the leaf, evaporation from the wet walls makes the air space around the mesophyll so much drier than the outside air that a steep drop occurs there, and that step is what generates the tension holding the whole column. The belief that gravity alone does the work fails because gravity opposes upward movement, so it cannot itself supply the gradient that makes water rise, and the belief that every step is at one potential fails because water only moves from a higher to a lower water potential.
questions.hint: Ask which step actually creates the tension that the whole column hangs on.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain what a gas bubble in a xylem conduit does to the water column
questions.stem: A drought-stressed tree browns and dies branch by branch from the top down, and sections of the dead wood show gas bubbles in the vessels. What does that show has happened?

options.text: A conduit lost its water column to vapour, so the tension could no longer be transmitted through it
Larvae tunnelled through the vessel walls from the inside and left the hollow passages behind
options.misconception: reads the bubbles as insect damage and dismisses the physical failure

options.text: Sap froze, expanded, and split the vessel walls along the grain of the wood
options.misconception: substitutes frost splitting for embolism without any freezing being described

options.text: Salt crystallised in the vessels until the passages were completely blocked by solid
options.misconception: treats a vapour-filled vessel as a salt-precipitation problem

questions.explanation: A conduit is only a pipe if it is full. Under strong tension the water in a vessel can pull away from itself and flash to vapour, and the resulting gas bubble is an embolism: the column is broken, so tension can no longer be transmitted past that point, the tissue beyond it stops receiving water, and it dies. The pit membranes between adjacent conduits normally stop one bubble from emptying its neighbours, which is why embolism spreads vessel by vessel rather than instantly. The reading of the bubbles as insect tunnels fails because the vessels described are on the conducting side of the wood, and the salt reading fails because a filled vessel would show solid on sectioning rather than a gas space.
questions.hint: Ask what a pipe full of water stops being if the water inside it becomes vapour.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain why root pressure cannot account for a tall tree's height
questions.stem: In very wet soil, a cut stump exudes sap for hours and the sap rises above the cut. Why can this not be the mechanism that supplies a 40 metre tree?

options.text: It is too weak to beat gravity but strong enough to push water back out through the leaf surface
options.misconception: claims the water reappears at the leaves, inverting where the water is lost

options.text: It happens only in dead wood, so a living stem with an intact crown can never produce it
options.misconception: assigns the effect to dead wood, where no ion pumping is possible at all

options.text: It is created by the same leaf evaporation that drives the transpiration stream in the xylem
options.misconception: conflates a positive osmotic pressure with the negative tension of transpiration

options.text: It needs the living root to pump ions in, so it adds pressure rather than tension and cannot lift water high

questions.explanation: Root pressure is positive pressure generated osmotically: the living root takes ions into the xylem, water follows by osmosis, and the xylem is pushed outward, which is why a stump weeps. Because it is a positive pressure it can only push water up to the height that pressure balances, which is of the order of ten metres, and it needs a metabolising root, so it stops whenever the root is cold or droughted. The main mechanism over great height is the negative pressure set at the leaf, which is a pull rather than a push and has no such height ceiling. The belief that root pressure is the same thing as transpiration fails because one raises pressure below the cut and the other lowers it above the leaves.
questions.hint: Ask whether the mechanism adds pressure or removes it, and what that does to the height limit.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Transpiration rate from a measured loss
questions.learningObjective: convert a potted water loss into a rate per unit leaf area
questions.stem: A potted plant with 2500 square centimetres of leaf is weighed, and the soil surface is covered to stop evaporation from the pot. Seven days later the pot has lost 350 grams. What is the transpiration rate?

options.text: About 500,000 grams per square metre per day, which is the same figure untreated
options.misconception: treats the square centimetre figure as if it were already per square metre

options.text: About 200 grams per square metre per day
About 2000 grams per square metre per day, which is what a wrong area gives
options.misconception: converts 2500 square centimetres to 0.025 square metres instead of 0.25

options.text: About 1400 grams per square metre per day, which omits the step for days
options.misconception: divides the seven-day total by area but never divides by the seven days

questions.explanation: The loss over the week is 350 grams, so the average daily loss is 350 divided by 7, which is 50 grams per day. The leaf area of 2500 square centimetres is 2500 times 1e-4, which is 0.25 square metres, so the rate per unit area is 50 divided by 0.25, which is 200 grams per square metre per day. Checking the three numbers in a different order, 350 divided by 7 divided by 0.25 gives the same 200, and the figure that appears if the days are forgotten, 350 divided by 0.25, is 1400, seven times too large. Covering the soil matters because without it the same 350 grams would include direct evaporation from the pot surface.
questions.hint: Turn the week into days and the square centimetres into square metres before dividing.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Water use efficiency from two measurements
questions.learningObjective: compute a water use efficiency and check it against a second measurement
questions.stem: In one trial a plant lost 350 grams of water and gained 0.875 grams of dry matter. In a second trial it lost 70 grams of water and gained 0.175 grams. What is the water use efficiency in each trial?

options.text: 1400 in the first and 140 in the second, so efficiency falls as the plant grows
options.misconception: reads the seven-day total as a daily figure in the first trial only

options.text: 20 grams in the first and 400 in the second, so the second plant is far more efficient
options.misconception: divides by the first trial's dry mass in the second trial instead of its own

options.text: 400 grams of water per gram of dry matter in both, so the two trials agree
2.5 grams in both, which is the same ratio written in the opposite order
options.misconception: inverts numerator and denominator without changing the unit to match

questions.explanation: Water use efficiency is the water lost divided by the dry matter made, so the first trial gives 350 divided by 0.875, which is 400, and the second gives 70 divided by 0.175, which is also 400. The two trials therefore agree, and they agree for a structural reason: the second trial is the first scaled by a factor of five in both the water and the mass, and a ratio is unchanged when numerator and denominator are scaled together. The same two measurements written the other way round, dry matter per kilogram of water, give 0.875 divided by 0.35, which is 2.5 grams per kilogram, the same efficiency in other units.
questions.hint: Check whether one trial is a fixed multiple of the other in both numbers at once.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: identify what makes a tissue a source or a sink
questions.stem: A sugar beet stores sucrose in a swollen root. In midsummer that root is a sink, and after the plant has flowered the same root is a source. What has changed between those two states?

options.text: Whether the root's own sugar production exceeds what its own tissues consume
Whether the phloem can carry twice as much sugar in the autumn as in the summer
options.misconception: believes the conduit's carrying capacity changes with the season

options.text: Whether the xylem stream reverses so that sugar flows down the same tubes
options.misconception: reverses the xylem and confuses the two conduits once more

options.text: Whether the number of sieve tubes formed at the start of the season is large enough
options.misconception: treats a fixed tube count as something that can be exceeded or not

questions.explanation: A source is a tissue that releases sugar into the phloem, a sink is a tissue that removes sugar from it, and the same tissue can be one or the other at different times depending on the balance between what it makes and what it uses. A young root in midsummer imports sugar to grow, so it is a sink; after flowering the plant has finished growing and the root is storing, so it is a source. The belief that the conduits' capacity changes fails because sieve tube number and the transport machinery are set during growth, and the belief that the xylem reverses fails because water and sugar travel in separate systems in separate directions.
questions.hint: Ask whether the tissue is a net producer or a net consumer of sugar at that moment.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: name the mechanism that moves sucrose into the sieve tube
questions.stem: In a source leaf, sucrose is moved from the mesophyll into the sieve-tube companion cells, against a concentration gradient. How is that uphill step achieved?

options.text: By osmosis of water pushing a sugar solution bodily into the tube as a bulk flow
options.misconception: confuses osmotic water movement with the transport of a solute against a gradient

options.text: By simple diffusion, because the sieve tube always has less sugar than the mesophyll
options.misconception: assumes the concentration gradient always runs the way passive movement needs

options.text: By a carrier that runs on the hydrogen ion gradient a proton pump sets up in the plasma membrane
By bulk flow of xylem sap, which drags sugar along with the transpiration stream
options.misconception: routes phloem sugar into the xylem and reuses the transpiration stream

questions.explanation: Loading is active and indirect. A proton pump in the companion cell membrane uses energy to push hydrogen ions out, and the resulting electrochemical gradient drives a sucrose and hydrogen ion co-transporter inward, so sucrose accumulates in the companion cell against its own gradient. Water follows that sugar by osmosis, the sieve tube becomes pressurised, and the pressure gradient moves the sap onward. The belief that loading is passive fails because the concentration step is demonstrably uphill, and the belief that the transpiration stream carries sugar fails because the xylem carries water and minerals, and the two conduits are separate tubes.
questions.hint: Ask what the energy is spent on, and which ion gradient is being spent.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Pressure flow in a sieve tube
questions.learningObjective: state what drives bulk flow of phloem sap
questions.stem: A sieve tube runs between a source and a sink, and the sap moves from the source end to the sink end. What provides the driving force for that bulk flow?

options.text: An electrical pump that pulls solute along the tube from one end to the other
options.misconception: invents a dedicated pump inside the tube, confusing it with a proton pump at loading

options.text: A hydrostatic pressure difference, higher at the loaded source end than at the unloading sink end
The transpiration stream in the neighbouring xylem vessels, which drags sap along with it
options.misconception: reuses the xylem flow as the engine of phloem transport

options.text: Active contraction of the sieve-tube cells, which squeezes the sap from end to end
options.misconception: treats a living cell as a muscle that can contract and push its contents

questions.explanation: The pressure-flow description rests on a pressure difference. Loading sugar at the source lowers the water potential there, water enters by osmosis, and the sieve tube becomes pressurised. Unloading at the sink raises the water potential of the sink side, water leaves, and the pressure there falls. Sap then moves down the resulting hydrostatic gradient from high pressure to low. The belief that a pump inside the tube drives the flow fails because the tube itself is a conduit and not a pump, and the belief that living cells contract fails because sieve elements are alive but they move sap by pressure, not by muscular action.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to water on each side of the tube after sugar enters and leaves it.

questions.topic: Mass flow rate in a sieve element
questions.learningObjective: compute the mass of sucrose carried through one sieve element per hour

options.misconception: reads 171 grams per litre as a mass passed in an hour with no volume step

options.text: About 0.0054 milligrams, which is the same answer off by a factor of a thousand
options.misconception: converts the cross-section into square centimetres and forgets the matching unit change

options.text: About 54 milligrams, which comes from a thousand-fold slip in the volume step

questions.learningObjective: explain why unloading lowers the pressure inside a sieve tube
questions.stem: At a growing root tip, sucrose is removed from a sieve tube and used by the root. Why does that removal make the pressure inside the tube fall?

options.misconception: reverses both the water direction and the effect on pressure

questions.learningObjective: name the enzyme and the first acceptor in C3 carbon fixation
questions.stem: In the first step of carbon fixation in a C3 plant, carbon dioxide is added to a five-carbon sugar. Which pair names the enzyme and the acceptor?

options.text: Pyruvate with ribulose bisphosphate, a five-carbon sugar phosphate

questions.learningObjective: explain how a C4 plant reduces photorespiration at the cost of extra energy

options.text: Both separate them in time, but CAM does it in the dark and C4 does it in the light

options.misconception: forgets that each NADPH is reduced by two electrons rather than one

options.text: Four photons, since two electrons each need two photons and two NADPH are required
Eight photons, which doubles the count for the cyclic flow that makes the extra ATP
options.misconception: adds the cyclic flow requirement to the linear flow count

options.text: Six photons, which adds one photon per NADPH for the transport of each carrier
options.misconception: invents a transport cost per carrier that the reaction scheme does not contain

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ion fluxes that open a stoma
questions.learningObjective: sequence the ion and water movements that open a stoma
questions.stem: Put these four events in the order in which they occur in a guard cell as a stoma opens in daylight.

options.text: Hydrogen ions are pumped out of the guard cell by an enzyme in its membrane
The hydrogen ion gradient drives potassium and other solutes into the guard cell
The solute concentration of the guard cell rises, so its water potential falls
Water enters the guard cell by osmosis and the pore opens as the cells bow apart

questions.explanation: The pump has to go first, because the gradient it creates is what everything else uses. Pumping hydrogen ions out lowers the guard cell's water potential directly, and the electrochemical gradient that results then drives potassium and other solutes in through coupled transporters. Only once the internal solute concentration has risen enough to overcome the pressure already in the cell does water follow by osmosis. The final step is mechanical: the guard cell walls are unevenly thickened, with the thickened inner wall next to the pore unable to stretch as much as the thin outer wall, so as the cells swell they bow away from each other and the pore opens. The order cannot be reversed because there is no gradient to exploit before the pump runs.
questions.hint: Nothing can be driven by a gradient that has not been created yet.

questions.learningObjective: read a fall in stomatal conductance from a three-point temperature series

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): Leaf discs of the same plant were cut from the same leaf, blotted, and then enclosed in a sealed chamber at a known carbon dioxide concentration. The rate at which the carbon dioxide in the chamber fell was measured at three temperatures, with the discs equilibrated for twenty minutes at each temperature before the reading was taken. The results are 0.40 moles per square metre per second at 15 degrees Celsius, 0.90 at 25 degrees, and 0.60 at 35 degrees. A second batch of discs from the same leaf, treated identically but supplied with water instead of a closed chamber, showed the same values.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, what does the fall in conductance between 25 and 35 degrees tell you, and how large is it?

options.text: Conductance at 35 equals its 25 degree value, since both are in sealed chambers
options.misconception: assumes the apparatus rather than the physiology fixes the measured rate

options.text: Conductance at 35 is 60 percent of its 25 degree value, a fall of 40 percent
options.misconception: reads the 0.60 figure as a fraction instead of a value in the same units

options.text: Conductance at 35 is 150 percent of its 25 degree value, a rise of 50 percent
options.misconception: divides the smaller by the larger the wrong way round, inverting the trend

options.text: Conductance at 35 is two thirds of its 25 degree value, a fall of 33.3 percent

questions.learningObjective: state the drought signal that closes stomata and the route it takes
questions.stem: When a plant's soil dries, the first measurable response in the leaf is a fall in stomatal conductance within minutes. What is the signal that produces it?

options.text: Ethylene released by the senescing leaf, which triggers the guard cells to shut
options.misconception: substitutes a ripening hormone for the drought signal that acts in minutes

options.text: Abscisic acid made in the root and moved in the xylem, acting on the guard cell ion channels

options.misconception: uses a hormone whose normal role opposes the closure described here

There it triggers signalling that blocks the inward-rectifying ion channels in the guard cell, the anions and then potassium leave, the guard cell's water potential rises, water follows out, and the pore closes. The naming is misleading: abscisic acid is not what makes leaves drop, and the hormone that does is ethylene. The response is fast because xylem flow delivers the signal directly, without a slow step through the phloem.

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): Four cultivars of the same species were grown in two controlled cabinets at the same temperature, the same light intensity and the same carbon dioxide concentration, with only the length of the light period differing. Cultivar S1 flowered in 40 days under a ten hour day and not at all under a sixteen hour day. Cultivar S2 flowered in 44 days under the ten hour day and not at all under the sixteen hour day. Cultivar L1 did not flower under the ten hour day and flowered in 38 days under the sixteen hour day. Cultivar L2 did not flower under the ten hour day and flowered in 42 days under the sixteen hour day. Any plant that had not flowered by day 90 was recorded as not flowering and was discarded.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, how should the four cultivars be grouped, and what is the mean time to flower for the two that flowered under the ten hour day?

options.text: S1 and S2 are short-day, L1 and L2 long-day, and the mean of 40 and 44 is 42 days
S1 and L1 are short-day, S2 and L2 long-day, and the mean of 40 and 38 is 39 days
options.misconception: pairs by position in the list rather than by which cabinet produced a flower

options.text: All four are long-day, and the mean of all four times is 41 days
options.misconception: averages the times for cultivars that flowered in different cabinets

options.text: S1 and S2 are long-day, L1 and L2 short-day, and the mean of 38 and 42 is 40 days
options.misconception: reverses the groups and averages the wrong pair for the stated cabinet

questions.explanation: Only two cultivars flowered under the ten hour day and they are the ones that did not flower under the sixteen hour day, so by the definition S1 and S2 are short-day and L1 and L2 are long-day. The mean of the two ten hour flowering times is 40 plus 44 divided by two, which is 42 days. Two cautions about the table. The four not flowering entries are censored at 90 days, not real times, so they cannot enter a mean, and the two means are not directly comparable anyway because they were measured in different cabinets. What can be compared safely is which cabinet produced a flower, because everything else was held constant.
questions.hint: Group by the cabinet in which each cultivar flowered, then average only the two times from that cabinet.

questions.learningObjective: explain how unequal auxin distribution bends a shoot towards light
questions.stem: A coleoptile lit from one side bends towards that side, and a thin agar block placed on the shaded side collects more growth-promoting substance than one on the lit side. What does that show?

options.text: The substance stays level, and light simply weakens the cells on the side that is lit
options.misconception: assumes light has a direct damaging effect on cell elongation in coleoptiles

options.text: The growth substance moves to the lit side and inhibits those cells, so the shaded side outgrows them
options.misconception: puts the substance on the light side and makes light act directly as an inhibitor

options.text: The growth substance moves to the shaded side, where it makes those cells elongate more than the lit side
The substance moves to the shaded side and inhibits it, so the lit side elongates and bends away
options.misconception: gets the direction of transport right and the effect of the substance wrong

questions.explanation: The block assay is the decisive evidence because it measures the substance rather than inferring it. More of it arrives on the shaded flank, and on the shaded flank the cells elongate more, so the organ curves towards the light. The receptor that detects the light direction is a phototropin in the coleoptile tip, and the redistribution that follows is of the auxin that promotes elongation in shoots. Note the tissue dependence: in a root the same redistribution of the same hormone inhibits elongation on the shaded side instead, so a root curves away from the light, and that difference is a matter of what the hormone does in that tissue rather than of how it is transported.
questions.hint: Ask which side collected more of the substance, and which side then grew more.

questions.learningObjective: explain why a horizontally placed root bends downwards
questions.stem: A seedling is laid on its side in a dark box, and within an hour the root curves down while the shoot curves up. What has redistributed, and what does it do differently in the two organs?

options.misconception: reverses both the direction of transport and the tissue responses

options.text: Auxin has moved to the lower side, where it inhibits cell elongation in the root and promotes it in the shoot
Auxin has moved to the lower side and promoted elongation in both, so the root and shoot both curve up
options.misconception: predicts one response for both organs, which is what removes the opposite bending

Then the tissue response diverges. In a shoot, auxin promotes elongation, so the lower side grows more and the shoot curves upwards, which is a positive response to gravity. In a root, the same auxin at the same concentration inhibits elongation, so the lower side grows less and the root curves downwards, a positive response as well. The dual effect of one hormone in two tissues is what allows two organs on the same plant to point in opposite directions, and it is a useful warning against treating a hormone as a single effect.

questions.learningObjective: explain how the shoot tip suppresses the growth of lateral buds
questions.stem: A shoot tip is removed from a young plant and the two buds just below the cut begin to grow. What does the tip have been doing to them?

options.text: Releasing a volatile chemical that burns the buds it wishes to suppress
options.misconception: invents a destructive chemical where the effect is a change in bud competence

options.text: Supplying them with a constant stream of sugar that they need in order to grow at all
options.misconception: makes the tip a food supply, when the cut surface and the leaves also supply sugar

options.text: Drawing all the water to the tip, so the buds wilt until the tip is removed
options.misconception: substitutes a water flow argument for a hormonal one

options.text: Exporting auxin that keeps the lateral buds dormant, an effect that is indirect

questions.explanation: Apical dominance is a hormonal effect with a well known complication. The tip makes auxin and exports it down the stem, and the indirect mechanism is now reasonably well established: auxin arriving at a lateral bud represses the expression of the genes that would let the bud grow, including the cytokinin pathway that promotes it. So the tip does not starve the bud or poison it, and removing the tip removes the repression, the cytokinin pathway is no longer held down, and the bud grows. This is the reason fruit growers cut back hedges and espaliered trees, and it is also the reason that an intact leafy shoot is not simply a supply of sugar to the buds below it.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the buds when the source of the hormone is taken away, and by what route the hormone acts.

The name of the hormone describes its first discovered effect, promoting cell division in culture, which is why it is often used to release lateral buds in tissue culture, and rooting compounds sold for cuttings contain a synthetic auxin precisely to suppress the buds and force root formation instead. questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain how dormancy is imposed and lifted in a seed
questions.stem: A seed stays asleep in a packet for a year and then germinates within a week of being moved to damp, warm soil. Which hormone's change best accounts for the switch?

options.text: Abscisic acid rises, because a high level of it is what starts germination in soil
options.misconception: inverts the hormone's role, which is to maintain dormancy rather than to end it

options.text: Abscisic acid falls relative to the growth-promoting hormones, lifting the block on germination
Ethylene falls, since ethylene rather than abscisic acid is the inhibitor of germination
options.misconception: makes ethylene the inhibitor and places abscisic acid outside the control altogether

options.text: Cytokinin falls, since cytokinin has been shown to stop a seed germinating
options.misconception: reverses the role of the hormone that promotes cell division in the embryo

Abscisic acid is synthesised as the seed matures and it imposes dormancy by shutting down the embryo's own growth programme and by maintaining seed-specific proteins in the seed coat and in storage tissues that would otherwise let the embryo emerge. When the seed receives the right combination of signals, a fall in that inhibition relative to the growth hormones, together with water uptake, light and temperature, allows germination to begin. The hormone's name is a historical accident from work on leaf abscission and it is not a major abscission hormone, which is why it is better to read the mechanism than the name.
questions.hint: Ask whether the inhibitor rises or falls when the block is released.

questions.learningObjective: describe the autocatalytic ripening response to ethylene
questions.stem: One ripe apple in a closed bag of unripe fruit ripens the whole bag within days. What does that show about the ripening signal?

options.text: Ripening tissue makes ethylene that inhibits further ethylene synthesis in the rest of the bag
options.misconception: inverts the feedback, which is positive rather than negative

options.text: Ripening tissue makes a gas that is consumed by its neighbours, so the unripe fruit starve
options.misconception: turns a ripening signal into a nutrient depletion effect

options.text: Ripening tissue makes ethylene, and ethylene promotes ripening, so the signal amplifies itself
Ripening tissue makes water vapour, and the humidity softens the skin of the unripe fruit
options.misconception: gives the effect to humidity, which softens surfaces but does not reprogram them

Ethylene is that gas, and the response it triggers in ripening tissue includes the synthesis of more ethylene synthase, so the system is autocatalytic and the effect is exponential rather than linear. The same positive feedback explains two commercial facts: fruit is picked green and ripened with ethylene, and one rotten apple really does spoil a basket. questions.learningObjective: read a dose-response curve for a plant hormone treatment

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): Sections of oat coleoptiles of the same length were incubated in the dark for four days in 5 millilitres of nutrient solution, with the synthetic auxin concentration varied and everything else held constant. The mean increase in length of each section was measured. The concentrations tested were 0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1 and 1.0 moles per litre, and the mean increases were 2.0, 3.1, 7.4, 11.0 and 4.2 millimetres respectively. Each value is the mean of ten sections, and the standard error of each mean was below 0.4 millimetres.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, at which concentration is the response greatest, and how much of the peak is lost at the highest concentration tested?

options.text: At 0.1 moles per litre, where 11.0 of 11.0 millimetres is achieved, and 16.2 percent is lost at 1.0
options.misconception: compares the high dose with the control instead of with the peak

options.text: At 1.0 moles per litre, where 4.2 of 11.0 millimetres is achieved, and 61.8 percent is lost at 0.1
options.misconception: locates the peak at the last dose and turns the fall into the loss

options.text: At 0.01 moles per litre, where 7.4 of 11.0 millimetres is achieved, and 33.0 percent is lost at 1.0
options.misconception: picks the third dose and measures the loss against the wrong reference value

options.text: At 0.1 moles per litre, where 11.0 of 11.0 millimetres is achieved, and 61.8 percent is lost at 1.0

questions.explanation: The largest mean increase is 11.0 millimetres, and it occurs at 0.1 moles per litre, so that is the optimum in the range tested. At 1.0 moles per litre the response is 4.2 millimetres, and the loss measured against the peak is 11.0 minus 4.2, which is 6.8, and 6.8 divided by 11.0 is 61.8 percent. Measuring the same fall against the control instead gives 4.2 divided by 2.0, which is 210 percent of control, and the difference between 100 and 210 is the same 110 percentage points, which is why the reference has to be stated. The pattern is a classic biphasic dose response: promotion at low concentrations and inhibition at high ones, in the same tissue and with the same hormone.
questions.hint: State the reference value before computing any percentage loss, and pick the largest mean.

questions.topic: Meristem division and the doubling of a cell number
questions.learningObjective: compute a cell number from a number of mitotic divisions
questions.stem: One cell of a root meristem divides ten times in a day, every division being synchronous. How many cells does that one cell produce?

options.misconception: multiplies linearly instead of exponentially

options.text: 1024, which is 2 raised to the power of 10
100, which counts the divisions without doubling the population each time
options.misconception: counts events rather than the cells those events produce

options.text: 20, which adds one cell per division and ignores the cells already present
options.misconception: adds one per division rather than doubling what is already there

questions.explanation: Each division replaces one cell with two, so the population doubles at every step and the total after n divisions is 2 to the power of n. questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain why a plant withdraws nutrients from old leaves before they fall
questions.stem: A plant growing in a nutrient-poor soil still sends nitrogen out of its oldest leaves and into new growth, and the old leaves yellow and drop. Explain what makes that transfer worthwhile rather than wasteful.

answer.exemplar: The transfer is worthwhile because the plant is a single connected system and the newest growth is the part that will reproduce. Nitrogen and several other elements can be pulled out of old leaves and carried to young leaves, whereas the structural material of the leaf, notably the cellulose of the cell walls and the structural proteins of the chloroplast, cannot be remobilised and is abandoned. The chlorophyll breaks down as a result, and the yellowing is the chlorophyll going, which is why a yellowing old leaf is a sign of remobilisation rather than of damage. A nutrient-poor soil makes the transfer more valuable, not less, because the alternative to exporting a mobile nutrient from an old leaf is leaving it in a leaf whose photosynthetic output is already falling. The resorption is a real saving, but it is partial and it is bounded: it cannot rescue a plant grown without nitrogen, and the nutrients are worth reclaiming because a large fraction of the nitrogen in a plant is in leaf protein, most of it in the machinery of photosynthesis, and that machinery is replaced every few days. What makes the pattern diagnostic is that the mobile elements leave the old leaves first and the immobile ones stay, which is exactly the order in which a deficiency shows, so the yellowing of old leaves is a symptom the plant is recycling rather than a symptom it is dying of.

questions.explanation: Mobility is the key idea, and it is measurable in the order in which a shortage shows. Elements such as nitrogen, potassium and magnesium can be withdrawn from old leaves, moved in the phloem to young tissue and reused, so a plant grown without one of them shows the symptom on its oldest leaves first. Elements such as calcium and iron cannot be moved out of a leaf once deposited, so a shortage of one of those shows on the youngest leaves, and the plant cannot recycle it at all. The structural components of a senescing leaf, above all its cell wall cellulose, are not recoverable either, so the leaf is a one-off cost. The recycling is therefore a genuine saving on the most expensive part of the plant, the photosynthetic machinery, and it explains why a plant can persist for weeks on its own stored nitrogen before it flowers.
questions.hint: Ask which elements can leave an old leaf and which are locked in its structure for good.

questions.learningObjective: match each macronutrient to the molecule it forms part of
questions.stem: Which of these pair a macronutrient with the compound of which it is a structural part? Select all that apply.

options.text: Nitrogen, which is in the amine group of every amino acid
Phosphorus, which is in the phosphate group of ATP and of nucleic acids
Magnesium, which sits at the centre of the chlorophyll molecule
Potassium, which is a structural part of the cell wall as calcium pectate
options.misconception: assigns the wall's pectate role to potassium, which is the mobile osmotic cation instead

questions.explanation: Three of the four pairings are structural and correct. Nitrogen is in the amine group of every amino acid, so a protein anywhere in the plant needs it, and it is also in the amide of the chlorophyll macrocycle. Phosphorus is in the phosphate of every nucleotide, so it is required for both ATP and the nucleic acids, and for membrane phospholipids. Magnesium is the metal ion at the centre of the chlorophyll molecule, which is why its deficiency causes interveinal chlorosis even though the veins stay green. The fourth pairing fails because it is calcium, not potassium, that cross-links the pectate in the middle lamella of the cell wall; potassium is present as a free cation, is highly mobile, and has no structural role in the wall.

questions.learningObjective: compute the reducing power needed to convert nitrate to ammonium
questions.stem: A root reduces nitrate to ammonium before the nitrogen can be built into amino acids. Nitrogen is at oxidation state plus five in nitrate and minus three in ammonium. How many electrons does one nitrate ion need, and how many NADPH does that represent?

options.misconception: keeps the correct electron count and misstates the NADPH stoichiometry

options.text: Two electrons, which is one NADPH, since the nitrogen drops by two oxidation states

Hydrogen counts 10 on the left as 4 plus 6 on the right, and the charges balance at plus one on both sides. Since each NADPH donates two electrons, eight electrons is four NADPH equivalents, of which the first is used by the cytosolic nitrate reductase and the rest arrive as reduced ferredoxin. The count of three oxygen atoms is irrelevant to the electron count, which follows the oxidation state and not the number of oxygens.

options.misconception: reverses the tough outer coat with the thin inner one

options.text: The outer ring is the exine, the inner ring is the intine, and the small circles are the two nuclei

questions.explanation: A pollen grain has two walls. The exine is the outer one, tough and chemically resistant because it is made of sporopollenin, which is why fossil pollen is so abundant in sediments and why the exine's surface pattern is used to identify pollen to species. The intine is the thin inner wall of cellulose and pectin, and it is through this layer, at an aperture where the exine is thinned, that the pollen tube pushes out. The two small circles in the cytoplasm are the nuclei, the tube nucleus which directs growth and the generative nucleus. In the common three-celled grain the generative nucleus has already divided into two sperm cells before the grain is shed, so a single grain delivered to the stigma carries two sperm to the ovule.
questions.hint: Ask which wall has to survive strong acid during pollen tube studies.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Pollen tube growth to the ovule
questions.learningObjective: identify and correct a wrong account of how a pollen tube reaches the ovule
questions.stem: A student writes that a pollen grain lands on the stigma and a tube grows straight down the style to the ovary wall, where it stops and releases the sperm. Which correction addresses the account as written?

options.text: The tube is guided by gravity, and it enters the ovule through the stalk that attaches it to the plant
options.misconception: replaces chemical guidance with gravity and names the funiculus instead of the micropyle

options.text: The tube is guided by a chemical signal from cells at the ovule's opening and enters through the micropyle, not the wall
The tube only begins to grow once the sperm have been released from the grain at the stigma
options.misconception: reorders the sequence, putting sperm release before the tube grows at all

options.text: The tube is a rigid extension of the wall, so it does not grow by tip growth and needs no signal
options.misconception: denies tip growth, which is what makes guidance by signal necessary

questions.explanation: The error is a missing guidance mechanism, and its absence is what makes the account implausible. A tube grows by tip growth along a precisely controlled path through the style, which requires the tip to be directed by a signal, and the target is the ovule's opening, the micropyle. The signal comes from the two synergid cells beside the egg, which attract the tube, and the tube enters the embryo sac through that opening and releases its two sperm there. The belief that gravity guides the tube fails because a tube growing towards a downward-directed ovule would be the wrong direction, and the belief that the sperm are released first fails because there is nowhere to release them until the tube has arrived.
questions.hint: Ask what the tube is aiming at, and what tells the growing tip which way to go.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: state the two products of the two fusions in double fertilisation
questions.stem: A diagram shows an embryo sac with a large central cell holding a fused diploid nucleus, and below it an egg cell flanked by two smaller cells at the ovule's opening. Two sperm cells from one pollen tube have entered the sac. What do the two sperm do, and what are the two products?

options.text: One fuses with the egg to make a diploid zygote, the other with the polar nuclei to make triploid endosperm
Both fuse with the egg, so the two zygotes grow into the embryo and into the cotyledons
options.misconception: makes both fusions with the same cell and splits the embryo's own parts

options.text: One fuses with the egg, the other degenerates, and the endosperm grows from the ovule wall
options.misconception: makes the second sperm a spare and reassigns the endosperm to maternal tissue

options.text: One fuses with the polar nuclei, the other with the nucellus, which then becomes the seed coat
options.misconception: swaps the partners and turns the innermost ovule tissue into the seed coat

questions.explanation: Double fertilisation is the event that makes an angiosperm an angiosperm, because one pollen grain supplies both the embryo and its food supply. The first sperm fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote, which is the embryo. The second fuses with the two polar nuclei, which have already fused to form a diploid nucleus in the central cell, so the endosperm nucleus is triploid. The endosperm is therefore genetically different from the embryo, being three sets of chromosomes rather than two, and it is a tissue peculiar to angiosperms, which is a large part of the fossil record argument about their origin. The cells beside the egg are the synergids, which guide the tube and are destroyed once the sperm arrive.
questions.hint: Count the chromosome sets: the egg contributes one, the sperm one, the polar nuclei two.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: The angiosperm life cycle: the female side
questions.learningObjective: order the steps from a megaspore mother cell to an embryo
questions.stem: Put these five events in the order in which they occur on the female side of an angiosperm's life cycle.

options.text: A diploid megaspore mother cell forms inside an ovule and divides by meiosis
Three of the four haploid megaspores degenerate and one survives
The surviving megaspore divides by mitosis without the chromosomes copying again
The result is an embryo sac of eight nuclei, with egg and polar nuclei at the open end
After fertilisation the zygote divides by mitosis to form an embryo inside the retained ovule

questions.explanation: The order follows from what each division does to the chromosome number. The megaspore mother cell is diploid, so its meiosis yields four haploid megaspores, of which three degenerate. The survivor then divides by mitosis three times, and mitosis copies the chromosomes before each division without halving them, so the result is eight haploid nuclei, not four, arranged with three antipodals at the far end and, at the open end, the egg cell, the two synergids and the two polar nuclei. Only after the pollen tube delivers a sperm does anything fuse, and the diploid zygote then builds the embryo by mitosis while the ovule is retained and becomes the seed.
questions.hint: Track the ploidy at each step, and remember that mitosis doubles the nucleus count without halving it.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Endosperm and the seed's food reserve
questions.learningObjective: explain why endosperm persists in some seeds and not in others
questions.stem: A cereal seed is mostly starchy endosperm when it is harvested, while a bean seed at the same stage has two large cotyledons and almost no endosperm. What accounts for the difference?

options.text: Both have endosperm, and the bean's is simply hidden inside the cotyledons rather than absent
options.misconception: denies the difference in tissue while conceding the visible difference in amount

options.text: The cereal is a monocot and cannot form endosperm, so its reserve is really cotyledon tissue
options.misconception: removes the tissue the cereal seed actually stores its reserve in

options.text: The bean is a dicot and stores reserve in its endosperm, which later moves into the cotyledons at germination
options.misconception: places the reserve in the wrong tissue and gives it the wrong timing

options.text: In the bean the endosperm is absorbed by the cotyledons before the seed dries, in the cereal it is not

questions.explanation: The endosperm is produced in both, and what differs is what happens to it afterwards. In many dicot seeds the endosperm is digested during maturation and its carbon, nitrogen and minerals are moved into the cotyledons, which are therefore the food reserve the seedling draws on. In cereal seeds the endosperm survives drying and is the reserve itself, packed with starch and with protein concentrated in its outer layer, which is why cereal bran is a valuable by-product. The transfer has a cost: a plant that stores its reserve in the seed's own tissue must build that tissue first, whereas a plant that keeps endosperm has a small seed and a large, rapidly growing nutritive tissue instead. Both arrangements deliver the same total carbon to the seedling.
questions.hint: Ask whether the endosperm is still present at the moment the seed is harvested.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: interpret a fruit-set experiment that separates self from cross pollination

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): Six groups of 200 flowers each were treated in one growing season on plants of the same clone, so all groups shared the same genotype apart from the pollen source. Group one was left unpollinated, group two was pollinated with its own pollen, and group three was pollinated with pollen from another plant of the same clone. Groups one to three were scored after twelve weeks. The unpollinated group set no fruit. The self-pollinated group set 96 fruit. The cross-pollinated group set 168 fruit. No other variable was changed, and every flower in a group received the same treatment.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, what do the three fruit-set percentages of 0, 48.0 and 84.0 show about the plant's breeding system?

options.text: Pollination is required, but the plant accepts its own pollen as well as foreign pollen
options.misconception: treats the 36 point shortfall as sampling scatter rather than a real effect

options.text: Pollination is required, and the plant rejects its own pollen, since selfing gives well under the crossed figure
The plant is self-compatible and cross-incompatible, since only the selfed group set fruit at all
options.misconception: reverses which treatment succeeded and omits that both set some fruit

options.text: Fruit set depends on how many pollen grains land, and no breeding system is indicated by these numbers
options.misconception: denies that the pollen source itself can change the outcome

questions.explanation: The three percentages are 0 out of 200, 96 out of 200, which is 48.0, and 168 out of 200, which is 84.0, and 264 fruit from 600 flowers, which is 44.0 overall. Two things are established. Pollination is required, since the unpollinated group set none at all. And self pollen is partly rejected, because 48.0 against 84.0 is a shortfall of 36 percentage points, and a shortfall of that size in 200 flowers is far beyond the scatter the design allows. The partial set rather than a complete absence is normal for many self-incompatible plants, since rejection depends on the pollen grain's own genotype and a plant has more than one pollen genotype, so some self pollen is accepted. The cross being from the same clone isolates the breeding system from any difference in plant quality.
questions.hint: Compare the two pollinated groups with each other rather than with the control alone.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: design a test that distinguishes a wind-dispersed from an animal-dispersed fruit
questions.stem: A botanist claims that a hooked fruit is dispersed by animals rather than by wind. Design an experiment that would support or undermine the claim, and say what the result would mean.

answer.exemplar: The claim is about two things at once, the mechanism and the agent, so the design has to separate them. Start with a null that could be wrong: that the hooks have no effect on where the fruit ends up, and that the fruit would travel just as far without them. For the first, present fruits in a standardised way, for example on the same release stand, with one group of intact hooked fruits and one group whose hooks have been carefully removed and the rest of the fruit left untouched, keeping fruit size, mass and release height constant, and then measure where each fruit lands, giving at least twenty replicates per group because landing position is variable. If hooked fruits travel significantly further, the hook is doing work, and if they do not, the hook is decoration. For the agent, run two parallel series that differ only in what can reach the fruit: one in a bare arena in which no animal has access and one in an arena in which a bird or mammal of the species suspected can reach the fruit, with the animal's own movements and any wind recorded, and then measure the distances travelled and whether the fruit passed through a gut. Seeds that survive that passage intact are the strong evidence, since digestion would destroy a seed that is merely dropped. What would undermine the claim is hooked fruit travelling as far as hookless ones in a wind-only arena, together with the fruit being recovered intact and undigested far from the parent, since that combination points to wind rather than to an animal.

questions.explanation: A good design here has a control that isolates the feature under test and a manipulation that isolates the agent. Comparing intact fruits with fruits whose hooks alone have been removed, at the same release height and in the same wind, tests what the hooks contribute rather than what the fruit's shape or weight contributes. Testing the same fruits with and without access by an animal of the candidate species tests the agent, and requiring evidence of gut passage, such as intact seeds recovered from droppings, rather than mere presence nearby, tests whether the animal actually dispersed them. Repeating each group is needed because wind is variable, and the two series must be run from the same release point so that distance travelled is comparable. The honest result is bounded: the experiment would establish which agent moved the fruit and whether the hook changed the outcome, but it would not by itself establish the evolutionary origin of the structure.
questions.hint: Change one feature of the fruit at a time, then change only whether an animal can reach it.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Fern life cycle and alternation of generations
questions.learningObjective: order the stages of a fern's life cycle by dominant generation
questions.stem: Put these five stages in the order in which they occur in the life cycle of a fern.

options.text: A spore lands on soil and germinates into a small green gametophyte
Motile sperm swim over the gametophyte to the archegonium and fertilise an egg
The diploid zygote divides by mitosis and grows into the familiar frond-bearing plant
On the underside of each frond, sporangia form in sori and release haploid spores
A diploid spore mother cell in a sporangium divides by meiosis to make those spores

questions.explanation: The fern alternates between a large diploid plant and a small haploid plant, and the cycle turns on which stage makes spores by meiosis. Starting from a spore, the small green gametophyte grows, its archegonia produce eggs and its antheridia release motile sperm that need free water to swim, and the diploid zygote that results divides by mitosis into the large fern plant, which is the dominant generation. The sporangia on the underside of its fronds contain spore mother cells, and their meiosis produces haploid spores, which closes the loop back to a gametophyte. The dependence on free water for the sperm is the feature that separates the fern from a seed plant, since a seed plant delivers its own sperm by pollen tube and does not need external water.
questions.hint: Start from the spore and follow the cycle round, keeping track of ploidy at each step.
